result.target_topic: Definition and Identification of Variable Interest Entities
result.target_summary: The company defines a variable interest entity (VIE) based on ASC Topic 810 criteria, specifically if equity is insufficient for financing without subordinated support or if equity investors lack significant decision-making power or proportional risk/return absorption. Investors holding debt, equity, guarantees, or specific fee/derivative arrangements are considered variable interest holders.

comparisons.peer_topic: Definition and consolidation criteria for VIEs
comparisons.peer_summary: The Corporation consolidates a Variable Interest Entity (VIE) if it has the power to direct the VIE's most significant economic activities and an obligation to absorb losses or right to receive significant benefits, reassessing this status quarterly.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and BAC define VIEs based on ASC Topic 810 criteria regarding insufficient equity or lack of controlling equity interests. C identifies a VIE if equity is insufficient for financing without subordinated support or if investors lack decision-making power/proportional risk absorption. BAC defines a VIE similarly as an entity that 'lacks equity investors or whose equity investors do not have a controlling financial interest.' While C explicitly details the two specific criteria (insufficient equity or lack of power/absorption), BAC summarizes this as lacking a 'controlling financial interest through their equity investments.' Both firms focus on the sufficiency and control aspects of equity to determine VIE status.

sentences.text: An entity is a variable interest entity (VIE) if it meets either of the criteria outlined in Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 810, Consolidation, which are (i) the entity has equity that is insufficient to permit the entity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support from other parties, or (ii) the entity has equity investors that cannot make significant decisions about the entity's operations or that do not absorb their proportionate share of the entity's expected losses or expected returns.
A VIE is an entity that lacks equity investors or whose equity investors do not have a controlling financial interest in the entity through their equity investments.

comparisons.peer_topic: Definition and characteristics of Variable Interest Entities (VIEs)
comparisons.peer_summary: Variable interest entities (VIEs) are defined as entities that either lack sufficient equity to finance their activities without subordinated support from other parties or have equity investors who cannot make significant decisions through voting rights, absorb expected losses, or receive residual returns.
comparisons.comparison: C and JPM provide nearly identical definitions of VIE criteria. C defines a VIE if (i) equity is insufficient to finance activities without subordinated support, or (ii) equity investors cannot make significant decisions or absorb proportionate losses/returns. JPM defines VIEs as entities that 'either (1) lack sufficient equity to permit the entity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support from other parties, or (2) have equity investors that do not have the ability to make significant decisions... or do not have the obligation to absorb the expected losses, or do not have the right to receive the residual returns.' The language and specific criteria for identifying a VIE are substantively the same.

sentences.text: An entity is a variable interest entity (VIE) if it meets either of the criteria outlined in Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 810, Consolidation, which are (i) the entity has equity that is insufficient to permit the entity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support from other parties, or (ii) the entity has equity investors that cannot make significant decisions about the entity's operations or that do not absorb their proportionate share of the entity's expected losses or expected returns.

VIEs are entities that, by design, either (1) lack sufficient equity to permit the entity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support from other parties, or (2) have equity investors that do not have the ability to make significant decisions relating to the entity's operations through voting rights, or do not have the obligation to absorb the expected losses, or do not have the right to receive the residual returns of the entity.
